problems.title: Co-rank by hand
hints: Merge by hand and count A's elements among the first k.

problems.title: Search cost

parts.prompt: Binary-search steps per co-rank (about log₂ n)?
Search steps as a fraction of merge steps per thread, in %?

problems.solution: 512 outputs per thread; 2 × 20 search steps = 7.8% overhead.

problems.title: Balanced by construction
problems.statement: A has 1,000 elements all smaller than B's 9,000 elements. 100 threads.

parts.prompt: How many threads read only A?

hints: The output is split evenly regardless of the data.
problems.solution: 100 outputs each; the first 10 threads take all of A, the other 90 all of B. Every thread does the same amount of work, unlike a split by input.

problems.title: Stability

parts.prompt: If B's equal keys went first, merge sort of records would…
options: lose stability: equal keys from the left run would move after those from the right

hints: Merge sort's stability comes from the merge.
problems.solution: A stable merge keeps left-run elements first on ties; that's what makes merge sort stable, which radix-style multi-key sorting relies on.

problems.title: Tiled merge traffic

parts.prompt: Minimum bytes (read A and B, write C)?

problems.solution: 256 MiB, 0.268 ms: the tiled (circular-buffer) merge reaches this; the basic one wastes sectors on scattered reads.

problems.title: Merge path
problems.statement: Merge path draws the merge as a path through an m × n grid.

parts.prompt: A thread's start point is where the path crosses…

problems.solution: The co-rank of k₀ is where the path crosses the diagonal i + j = k₀.

problems.title: Divergence in the merge loop

options: Lanes take different branches (A or B) depending on data
The body is short and the kernel is memory-bound

problems.solution: Each step's branch depends on the data; but the work per step is tiny and memory dominates.

problems.title: Co-rank invariants
problems.statement: For a valid co-rank i of k (with j = k − i).

options: i = 0 or j = n or A[i−1] ≤ B[j]
j = 0 or i = m or B[j−1] < A[i]

hints: The last A element taken can't be greater than the next B; the last B taken must be strictly less than the next A (ties go to A).
problems.solution: The two inequalities, with strictness chosen for stability; i ≤ k trivially.

problems.title: Circular buffers
problems.statement: The tiled merge loads tiles of A and B of size T and consumes them unevenly.

parts.prompt: What does the circular buffer avoid?
options: Re-loading the unconsumed part of a tile from global memory

problems.solution: Without it, each round reloads overlapping data; with it, every input element is read from global memory once.

problems.title: Generalising co-rank
problems.statement: Where else does "split the output evenly, binary-search the input boundaries" apply?

options: SpMV with uneven rows (split non-zeros evenly)

problems.solution: Merge-based SpMV and load-balanced graph traversal both use it.
